Similarly, EV adoption to date has been largely inaccessible to low-income populations due to the high cost of vehicles and EVSE, and a lack of charging infrastructure in areas where people with low incomes reside44. ChaaS has the opportunity to improve the equity of electric transportation by facilitating access to EV charging by low-income and otherwise underserved populations. This might be accomplished by improving adoption economics and streamlining processes. Specifically, ChaaS may be able to address the barriers that have limited the installation of charging infrastructure in MUDs, where people with low incomes are more likely to reside4546, as we demonstrate via a case study. If a ChaaS provider operates a network of charging infrastructure, this can also create an incentive to install and maintain infrastructure in areas where standalone infrastructure may not be economical due to low utilization. ChaaS networks thus serve to aggregate benefits of EVSE across users and communities. Finally, the various services of ChaaS can facilitate the decarbonization of electric transportation. While EVs produce zero tailpipe emissions, full decarbonization requires powering them with zero-carbon electricity. Many non-emitting electricity sources, such as wind and solar, can be difficult to integrate into the electric grid because their output is intermittent. In aggregate, EVs can serve as flexible loads by following the incentives of TOU rates, by participating in demand response programs, or even serving as storage resources via V2G, all of which can enable increased grid integration of intermittent power sources. Each of these functions is sufficiently complex that few EV adopters can feasibly participate without technical, automated support, which ChaaS providers are well suited to provide. As with any privately-operated entity providing services to the public, appropriate oversight will be necessary to enable equitable societal benefits and avoid unjust or monopolistic outcomes. For example, protecting ChaaS customers from unjustified price increases may require regulatory intervention, particularly if customers are contractually “locked in” to service from their ChaaS providers. Lessons learned from regulating electric utilities should serve as guidelines for developing a ChaaS regulatory framework.
